mainTopic: Advice and medical treatment from non-Jews and מינים, חיי שעה, and the limits of 'וחי בהם'
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier point: a Jew may ask a non-Jew for advice, because the non-Jew wants to protect his own reputation. Then רבי יוחנן rules on treatment by non-Jewish doctors. If it is unclear whether the patient will live or die, he may not be treated by them. If he will surely die without help, he may be treated by them, because we do not worry about losing חיי שעה. This is proved from the four מצורעים in מלכים ב. A ברייתא seems to argue: one may not be healed by מינים even for חיי שעה, as in the story of בן דמא. רבי ישמעאל stopped him from being healed by a מין, and he died. The גמרא answers that מינות is different because it can draw a person in. It also explains the 'snake' of the חכמים and why רבי ישמעאל rejected בן דמא's proof from 'וחי בהם': in public, one may not break the rule even to save a life. The amud ends with רבה בר בר חנה's two versions of which injuries may be treated by non-Jews, and the second version continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why asking a non-Jew for advice is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The non-Jew assumes he is being consulted like an expert who is asked by many people, so he gives good advice to protect his name.
steps.simpleTranslation: The non-Jew thinks: 'He is just asking my opinion. Just as he asks me, he will ask other people too.' If he gives bad advice, that man would only be hurting himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why it is permitted to ask a non-Jew for advice, even though we usually worry he might mean harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The non-Jew knows the Jew may check his advice with other people. If his advice turns out to be bad, his own reputation is ruined. Because of that self-interest, we can trust him to give honest advice.

keyTerms.meaning: He is simply asking (for an opinion)

steps.whatToRemember: Asking a non-Jew for advice is allowed because his own reputation is on the line.

phrases.english: He thinks: he is just asking him for his opinion,
phrases.notes: The one who 'thinks' here is the non-Jew being asked for advice.

phrases.english: just as he is asking him,
he will ask another person too,
and that man would end up harming himself.
phrases.notes: 'That man' is the non-Jew himself. Bad advice would ruin his own good name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes an explanation that began before this section, giving the reason asking advice is permitted.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the psychology of the non-Jew: self-interest guarantees honest advice.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought asking a non-Jew for advice is dangerous, since he may intend harm.
steps.terutzMaskana: He gives good advice because the Jew can check it with others, and bad advice would hurt his reputation.

steps.title: When a sick person may be treated by non-Jewish doctors
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules: if it is unclear whether the patient will live or die, no treatment from them. If he will surely die, he may be treated by them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן (some say רב חסדא said it in the name of רבי יוחנן): If it is uncertain whether he will live or die, we do not get treated by them. If he will surely die, we do get treated by them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from רבי יוחנן about getting medical care from non-Jewish doctors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is that a non-Jewish doctor might harm the patient. If the patient might recover anyway, that risk is not worth taking. If he will surely die without help, the doctor offers his only chance, so treatment is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Unclear whether he will live or die

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base ruling that the rest of the section questions and defends.

phrases.english: Rava said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said,
and some say: Rav Ḥisda said
that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
If it is uncertain whether he will live or die,
we do not get treated by them;
if he will certainly die, we do get treated by them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: medical treatment instead of advice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a case of doubt, no treatment from non-Jewish doctors. If death is certain without treatment, treatment is permitted.

steps.title: Challenge: a dying person still has some time left
steps.stepSummary: Even someone sure to die still has חיי שעה. Why risk losing that time?
steps.simpleTranslation: Certain to die? But he still has a short stretch of life left!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second half of רבי יוחנן's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A patient who will surely die still has some days or hours left. If the non-Jewish doctor harms him, he loses even that time. So why allow the risk?

keyTerms.meaning: Short-term life; the limited time a dying person has left

steps.confusionAlert: חיי שעה does not mean 'one hour.' It means whatever short time the patient has left before he dies.

phrases.english: Will die? But there is still short-term life!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the leniency in step 2 for the 'certain to die' case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that one who is certain to die may be treated by non-Jewish doctors.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Treatment risks cutting short the remaining life the patient still has, so it should be forbidden.

steps.title: We do not worry about חיי שעה
steps.stepSummary: When there is a chance of full recovery, we do not hold back to protect the short time left.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are not concerned about short-term life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chance of real, lasting recovery outweighs the risk of losing the short time left. So the dying patient may take the risk of treatment.

phrases.english: We are not concerned about short-term life.

steps.terutzResolutionType: States a governing principle that removes the concern.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Short-term remaining life must be protected, even at the cost of a chance to recover.
steps.terutzMaskana: חיי שעה is not a concern when there is a chance of full recovery.

steps.title: What is the source for not worrying about חיי שעה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source for the principle it just used.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do you say that we are not concerned about short-term life?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for proof of the principle. This sets up the next step, which brings a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 4 was only a statement. Now the גמרא wants a source showing it is true.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do you say this?

phrases.english: And from where do you say
that we are not concerned about short-term life?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a source for the principle stated in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source proving that we do not worry about חיי שעה.

steps.title: Proof from the four lepers
steps.stepSummary: The lepers risked their last days to go to the Aramean camp, showing we do not worry about חיי שעה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'If we say, Let us go into the city, there is famine in the city and we will die there.' But they still had short-term life! So it must be that we are not concerned about short-term life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by bringing a פסוק about lepers who took a big risk to survive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lepers were starving and would surely die. They chose to go to the enemy camp, where they might be killed right away, because there was also a chance to live. Since they gave up their remaining time for a chance at survival, we learn that חיי שעה is not a reason to hold back.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not so that...? (introduces the conclusion)

steps.whatToRemember: A person facing certain death may take a risky treatment that could save him, even though it might shorten the little time he has left.

phrases.english: As it is written: 'If we say: We will enter the city,'
'then the famine is in the city, and we will die there.'
phrases.notes: The verse goes on: so they chose to go to the Aramean camp, where they might live or be killed.

phrases.english: But there was still short-term life!

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לָאו לְחַיֵּי שָׁעָה לָא חָיְישִׁינַן.
phrases.english: Rather, is it not that we are not concerned about short-term life?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5 with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The principle that we do not worry about חיי שעה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים ב 7:4: the lepers risked immediate death at the Aramean camp rather than wait to die of hunger.

steps.title: A ברייתא forbids healing from heretics even for short-term life
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that says one may not do business with מינים or be healed by them, even when only חיי שעה is at stake. This seems to contradict רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: A person may not do business with heretics, and one may not be healed by them even for short-term life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack רבי יוחנן's ruling. The ברייתא forbids healing from מינים even in the exact case where רבי יוחנן allowed it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said that if the patient will surely die, he may be treated, and we do not worry about his חיי שעה. This ברייתא says 'even for חיי שעה' one may not be healed by מינים. That sounds like the opposite rule for the same situation.

keyTerms.meaning: Heretics, Jews who turned to false beliefs
Short-term life, the little time a dying person has left

phrases.english: They raised an objection:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יִשָּׂא וְיִתֵּן אָדָם עִם הַמִּינִין,
phrases.english: A person may not do business with heretics,
and one may not be healed by them
even for short-term life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling after it was supported by the lepers' story.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that someone who will surely die may be treated, ignoring חיי שעה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly forbids healing even when only חיי שעה is at stake, which is the very case רבי יוחנן permitted.

steps.title: The story of בן דמא and the snake bite
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא tells how בן דמא was bitten by a snake. A מין named יעקב איש כפר סכניא came to heal him, but רבי ישמעאל would not allow it, and בן דמא died while trying to bring a proof that it was permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident with בן דמא, רבי ישמעאל's nephew, who was bitten by a snake. יעקב of כפר סכניא came to heal him, but רבי ישמעאל did not let him. בן דמא said: 'רבי ישמעאל, my brother, let him heal me, and I will bring a verse from the Torah that it is permitted.' He did not manage to finish before his soul left him and he died.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a real story to show its rule in action. This story backs up the objection against רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A snake bite was deadly, so בן דמא was in a 'surely die' situation. Even so, רבי ישמעאל refused to let the מין treat him. That fits the ברייתא, which forbids this even for חיי שעה.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a true story brought as an example

phrases.english: There was an incident with ben Dama,
the son of Rabbi Yishmael's sister,
whom a snake bit,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא יַעֲקֹב אִישׁ כְּפַר סְכַנְיָא לְרַפּאוֹתוֹ,
phrases.english: and Yaakov, a man of the village of Sechanya, came to heal him,
phrases.notes: This יעקב was a מין, which is why the story belongs here.

phrases.english: but Rabbi Yishmael did not let him.
And he said to him:
phrases.notes: The speaker is בן דמא, talking to his uncle רבי ישמעאל.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, my brother!
Let him, and I will be healed by him,
and I will bring a verse from the Torah
that it is permitted.
But he did not manage to finish the statement
before his soul left him and he died.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבֶן דָּמָא בֶּן אֲחוֹתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the ברייתא's rule from step 7 with a real case.
steps.raayaObject: The ברייתא's rule that one may not be healed by a מין even for חיי שעה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of בן דמא, whom רבי ישמעאל stopped from being healed by יעקב איש כפר סכניא

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל praises בן דמא for dying in purity
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל calls בן דמא fortunate for dying pure, without breaking the חכמים' rule. He quotes the verse 'one who breaks a fence, a snake will bite him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל declared about him: Fortunate are you, בן דמא, for your body is pure and your soul left in purity, and you did not go against the words of your colleagues, who would say: 'And one who breaks a fence, a snake will bite him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל reacts to בן דמא's death by praising him. This shows that being healed by the מין would have been a real sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If treatment had been allowed, there would be nothing to praise. רבי ישמעאל calls it fortunate that בן דמא died without breaking the rule. That strengthens the objection: even a dying person may not be healed by a מין, which seems to go against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The words of your colleagues, meaning the rulings of the חכמים
One who breaks a fence, someone who ignores a protective rule of the חכמים

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael declared about him:
Fortunate are you, ben Dama,
for your body is pure
and your soul left in purity,
and you did not go against the words of your colleagues,
who would say:
"And one who breaks a fence, a snake will bite him."
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:8. The 'fence' is a protective rule of the חכמים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story from step 8 with רבי ישמעאל's verdict, which shows the treatment was truly forbidden.
steps.raayaObject: That healing from a מין is forbidden even when the patient is dying
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי ישמעאל's praise of בן דמא and the verse from קהלת 10:8
steps.whyThisMatters: This line turns the story into a clear legal proof. It shows the refusal was a real halachic requirement, not just caution.

steps.title: Heresy is different because it draws people in
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that מינות is a special case. Someone treated by a מין may be pulled toward his beliefs. That danger does not apply to an ordinary עובד כוכבים, so רבי יוחנן's ruling still stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Heresy is different, because it pulls people in, and he may come to be drawn after them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection by separating מינים from regular idolaters. רבי יוחנן's ruling is about idolaters, and the ברייתא is about heretics.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on healing from a מין is not about the medical risk to חיי שעה. It is about the spiritual risk of being drawn into heresy. So the ברייתא does not argue with רבי יוחנן: an ordinary idolater may treat a dying patient, but a מין may not.
steps.whatToRemember: A dying patient may be treated by an ordinary idolater (רבי יוחנן), but never by a מין. The reason is the danger of being pulled into heresy, not the risk to his short-term life.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the בן דמא story as saying חיי שעה must always be protected. The ban here is only because the healer was a מין.

phrases.english: Heresy is different, because it pulls people in,
since he may come to be drawn after them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection raised in steps 7 through 9 by limiting the ברייתא to heretics.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (heretic versus ordinary idolater)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and the story of בן דמא seemed to show that one may never risk חיי שעה by accepting treatment from outsiders.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban applies only to מינים, because heresy can draw a person in. Treatment by an ordinary idolater for a dying patient remains permitted, as רבי יוחנן ruled.

steps.title: But he was already bitten by a snake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי ישמעאל's words, 'a snake will bite one who breaks a fence', and asks: בן דמא was bitten by a snake anyway, so how was he spared?
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'You did not break your colleagues' words, who said: One who breaks a fence, a snake will bite him.' But he was also bitten by a snake!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line from the ברייתא and raises a problem with it. רבי ישמעאל said בן דמא was saved from the 'snake' of the פסוק, but a snake had already bitten him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל praised בן דמא for avoiding the punishment of 'a snake will bite him.' But the whole story began with a real snakebite. So what punishment did he avoid?

keyTerms.meaning: One who breaks a fence, meaning one who breaks a protective rule of the חכמים

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is going back to a line from the ברייתא in step 9.

phrases.english: You did not transgress the words of your colleagues,
who would say:
"And one who breaks a fence, a snake will bite him."
But he too was bitten by a snake!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבי ישמעאל's statement in step 9 and challenges how it fits the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's claim that בן דמא escaped the 'snake' punishment
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בן דמא was actually bitten by a snake, so he did not escape a snake.

steps.title: The snake of the Rabbis has no cure
steps.stepSummary: The 'snake' that punishes someone who breaks the חכמים' rules is different. It has no cure at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: The snake of the Rabbis is one that has no cure at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the snake in the פסוק is a special punishment that can never be healed. It is not like the ordinary snake that bit בן דמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן דמא's real snakebite could have been treated. The 'snake of the רבנן' is a punishment with no cure at all. By not breaking the rule, he was spared that worse punishment, so רבי ישמעאל's praise still makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The snake of the Rabbis', the punishment for breaking their rules

phrases.english: The snake of the Rabbis
is one that has no cure at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: חִוְיָא דְּרַבָּנַן דְּלֵית לֵיהּ אָסוּתָא כְּלָל
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The snake in the פסוק is an ordinary snake, which בן דמא did not escape.
steps.terutzMaskana: The snake in the פסוק is an incurable punishment, which בן דמא did escape.

steps.title: What proof did בן דמא want to bring?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which proof בן דמא was about to say before he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what was he going to say?
steps.whatsHappening: In the story, בן דמא died in the middle of bringing his proof. The גמרא now asks what that proof was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a clarifying question. It fills in a gap in the story so we can understand what the argument with רבי ישמעאל was really about.

keyTerms.meaning: What was he going to say?

phrases.english: And what was he going to say?
phrases.notes: That's בן דמא, who died before he could finish his proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי ישמעאל's words to the proof בן דמא was trying to give.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק בן דמא planned to use to show that healing by a מין was allowed

steps.title: 'He shall live by them', not die by them
steps.stepSummary: בן דמא would have quoted 'וחי בהם': the מצוות are for living, not for dying.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he shall live by them', and not that he should die by them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that בן דמא would have used the פסוק 'וחי בהם.' It teaches that one may break a rule to stay alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says a person should live through the מצוות. From this we learn that we do not keep a מצוה if it will cost a life. So בן דמא felt he could be healed by the מין to save his life.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he shall live by them', the source that saving a life comes before most prohibitions

phrases.english: "And he shall live by them"
and not that he should die by them.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בן דמא would have cited 'וחי בהם' to permit the healing in order to save his life.

steps.title: How would רבי ישמעאל answer that proof?
steps.stepSummary: If 'וחי בהם' allows breaking rules to save a life, why did רבי ישמעאל forbid the healing?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי ישמעאל? (How does he deal with this?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי ישמעאל did not accept this strong proof. This short question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'וחי בהם' seems to clearly allow saving a life. So it is hard to see how רבי ישמעאל could forbid it. The גמרא needs a reason that limits the rule.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yishmael?
phrases.notes: Short for: how would רבי ישמעאל answer the 'וחי בהם' proof?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses בן דמא's proof from step 14 to challenge רבי ישמעאל's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's refusal to let בן דמא be healed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'וחי בהם' allows breaking a rule to save a life, so the healing should have been allowed.

steps.title: Only in private, not in public
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל holds that 'וחי בהם' applies only in private. In public, one may not break the rule even to save a life.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only in private, but in public, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי ישמעאל agrees with 'וחי בהם', but only when the act is done in private. In public it does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is a limit on 'וחי בהם': private versus public. The גמרא's answer implies that רבי ישמעאל treated בן דמא's case as falling under the public side, so he did not allow the healing even though a life was at stake.

keyTerms.meaning: 'These words', meaning: this rule applies only when...

phrases.english: This applies only in private,
but in public, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי בְּצִינְעָא אֲבָל בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא לָא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'וחי בהם' permits breaking a rule to save a life in every situation.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי ישמעאל, 'וחי בהם' applies only in private, not in public.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל's ברייתא: private versus public
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי ישמעאל learns from 'וחי בהם' that one may even worship an idol to stay alive, but not in public, because of 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: רבי ישמעאל would say: From where do we know that if they tell a person 'Worship an idol and you will not be killed,' he should worship and not be killed? The verse says 'He shall live by them', not die by them. Could this be even in public? The verse says 'And you shall not profane My holy name.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבי ישמעאל really holds the private-versus-public rule from step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל applies 'וחי בהם' even to עבודה זרה, as long as it is in private. A second פסוק, 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי', teaches that in public one must not do it, because that would profane שם שמים. This matches the answer given for his ruling with בן דמא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One might think', raising a possibility that will be rejected
'And you shall not profane My holy name', the source for חילול השם

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל: 'וחי בהם' lets a person break even the prohibition of עבודה זרה to save his life, but only in private. In public, 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי' forbids it. That is why he did not let בן דמא be healed.
steps.confusionAlert: This is רבי ישמעאל's own view. Do not assume it is the final הלכה for every case. The point here is only to explain why he forbade the healing.

phrases.english: As it is taught:
Rabbi Yishmael would say:
From where do we know that if they say to a person
"Worship an idol and you will not be killed,"
that he should worship and not be killed?
The verse says: "And he shall live by them"
and not that he should die by them.
Could it be even in public?
The verse says:
"And you shall not profane My holy name."

steps.title: No non-Jewish treatment for injuries that override שבת
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה says in the name of רבי יוחנן: any injury serious enough to override שבת may not be treated by non-Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Any injury for which we break שבת, one may not be healed by them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new teaching about which injuries may be treated by non-Jewish healers. In this first version, dangerous injuries are the ones that may not be treated by them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An injury that overrides שבת is a life-threatening one. This version says that for such serious cases, one may not use a non-Jewish healer. A second version of the same teaching follows right away.

keyTerms.meaning: We break שבת for it, meaning it is life-threatening

steps.title: A second version of רבי יוחנן's teaching begins
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבה בר בר חנה's teaching in the name of רבי יוחנן differently. The new version starts here and continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Any...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a different version of the same teaching. The sentence is cut off here, so it sets up what comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ואיכא דאמרי' tells us the teaching was passed down in two ways. We need to see the rest of the sentence to know how this version differs from step 18.
